texts: Day 1 (4 Sep) — A long day
Japan to Canada via U.S.A.

The long-awaited day of departure. For this day I had lived frugally for half a year. On the winter trip to Canada a year and a half earlier we flew direct from Narita, but this time Centrair was our starting point. Via Narita and Portland in the USA, we were headed for Vancouver, Canada.

At Portland we had to change to a flight for Vancouver, but there was only a little over an hour to connect. Connecting in the USA means going through immigration, and there was a long queue that barely moved. Thinking we wouldn't make it, I told a staff member and they let us through with priority. To make things more annoying, we had to collect our bags once. The next flight was getting close, and we panicked. When we got to the gate, the electronic board showed a different airline from the one on our tickets, and outside sat a really small propeller plane. I was a bit worried, but the staff told us it was the right one. Apparently it's a partner of Delta. Changing planes twice is a hassle.
We arrived in good old Vancouver.

A year and a half ago you had to take a bus from Vancouver Airport to the city, but now the "Canada Line", a linear-motor train built for the Winter Olympics, can be boarded right outside the arrivals lobby. Very convenient.

We arrived in downtown Vancouver. Terribly sleepy... I wanted to relax at the hostel soon, but today's lodging wasn't in Vancouver, or even in Canada. To rent the car that would be our reliable partner on the long journey ahead, we had to cross the border to Seattle in the USA.

We went to Seattle not by plane but on Greyhound, the long-distance bus famous in the USA and Canada. Why do something so apparently pointless when we'd been in America only moments ago? Money. Renting a car was overwhelmingly cheaper in the USA than in Canada. For example, renting for three weeks in Canada would cost about 160,000 yen, partly because of an extra charge for being under 25. Rent in America, on the other hand, and it comes to about 100,000.

We took the bus to Seattle. When crossing the border, all the passengers have to get off the bus and go through immigration. You have to take your bags with you then, but I didn't understand and left them on the bus, which was embarrassing.

We arrived at the night's lodging. I hadn't slept at all on the plane or the bus, and the exhaustion was unreal. I feel like I'd been awake for about 30 hours... Mao was constantly fast asleep, but we were both tired.
Day 2 (5 Sep) — Across the border again, into Canada
to Kamloops

For all our exhaustion, one night's sleep made it strangely vanish. Seattle's cool breeze was refreshing. It was hard to believe that only yesterday we had been in sweltering Japan. Last night we stayed at Seattle City Hostel. Even though it's in the city centre near the bus depot, it's relatively cheap. About a ten-minute walk from the hostel is the Budget rent-a-car office. It was quite busy, but only one man was dealing with customers, so we had a long wait. Our partner for these three weeks was not an American car.

We stopped for a toilet break after driving for just under two hours. The photo on the right is our partner, a Hyundai Elantra!! We had asked for a compact car and never expected to be lent one this big. The 1.8 L engine had power to spare, and it even had cruise control. It was quiet too; no complaints at all. Its fuel economy, as we later found out, was 15 km/L, as good as a Japanese car. When I rented a Hyundai in Okinawa before, it was a saloon but felt like a non-turbo kei car, all noise and no power. To think Hyundai had come this far... The Koreans are formidable.
Heading north on Highway 5 for a while, we came back to the border we had crossed by bus. It looks just like a toll gate on a Japanese expressway.

In Vancouver we stopped at Mountain Equipment Co-op (MEC), the outdoor shop that also helped us on the trip a year and a half ago, and bought what we needed for hiking. On top of backpacks and boots we got a frying pan and bear bells, so we were fully prepared. The MEC-brand pack I fell for because of its name: the Alpine Light. The 60 L size cost about 14,000 yen. Very good quality, and I liked it. Waterproof zips, stylish check-patterned fabric, sides that open wide; I'd never seen anything like it among the cheap products sold in Japan. Canada, where you can buy good gear cheaply, is heaven for hikers.

From Vancouver we drove east for a while along Trans-Canada Highway 1. Unlike America there were few cars, and it was easy driving. From the west coast we headed into the interior of the North American continent. In the suburbs I handed the wheel to Mao. We had both got international driving permits for driving in Canada.

Drive about 300 km from Vancouver along the Fraser River and you reach the town of Kamloops. We stayed here for the night. We bought sushi at a nearby supermarket, Save-On-Foods, and had it for dinner.
Day 3 (6 Sep) — Into the heart of the Canadian Rockies
to Mt. Robson Provincial Park

Today we headed for Mt. Robson, in the heart of the Canadian Rockies, which run north–south along the border between British Columbia and Alberta. A commemorative photo outside the motel with our new backpacks.

After driving for a while it started to rain. We were starting our hike tomorrow; would it be OK? Kamloops is a junction town, with one road heading east to Banff and another toward Jasper, where we were going.

Today's leg was short. After a little over 300 km we reached the visitor centre at the foot of Mt. Robson, today's destination. The rain that had kept falling since we set off had almost stopped by the time we got here. But the ground around was still wet, and Robson was hidden in cloud. All we could do was pray for sun tomorrow. There are no shops here; it isn't a town. We thought we'd pitch the tent somewhere, but the car park said camping was prohibited. It's something we often did in Japan, so we were thrown, and decided to look for a campground nearby. The campground that should have been right nearby wasn't there, so we drove a little way.

Robson Meadows campground was laid out in patches through the primeval forest. It didn't feel like an open field; each site had a parking space big enough for a camper van and a space for a tent behind it, quite far from the next site, so even chatting until midnight wouldn't bother anyone. The atmosphere was completely different from Japanese campgrounds, so at first we were quite confused. For a start, we hadn't booked. There was no staff anywhere, so we might get told off for camping without permission. When we asked some people who had come in a camper van, they said the staff would come by car eventually, and we should camp at a site marked Available. We pitched the tent straight away. After a while a staff member did come by car and collected the money. I think it was about 800 yen each. For dinner, Mao deliciously cooked salmon fillets we had bought in advance at Save-On-Foods in Kamloops, dressed with a cream sauce for fish. From tomorrow, the hike at last.
What surprised us at this campground wasn't only the space. The toilets were flushing, and there was even a shower room with hot water. Free for guests. What a luxurious campground.
Day 4 (7 Sep) — Robson, mountain of glaciers
Mt. Robson
When we woke up, a clear blue sky was waiting. Unfortunately Mt. Robson was still hidden in cloud, but imagining the views that would greet us, our hearts swelled with anticipation.

Our starting point was the Berg Lake Trailhead. A long way of about 20 km from here. Cross the bridge over the Robson River and the trail begins in dense coniferous forest. This is already grizzly bear habitat.

After walking for a while the clouds cleared and the whole of Robson was revealed. What a divine mountain face. I can't imagine where you'd even start climbing it, but every year it's the stage where skilled alpinists aim for the summit. Of course we don't have the ability to aim for the peak. Our destination was Berg Lake, an emerald-green lake on the north side of Robson formed by glacier meltwater. The trail wraps around the west side of Robson to reach the back of the mountain.
Maple leaves, the leaf on Canada's flag, already turning yellow. Last night before bed and this morning when we woke it had been quite cold. Autumn seems to have already come here.
On the west side of Robson is the river flowing from Berg Lake. The water wasn't clear, but it was a beautiful emerald green.

Kinney Lake, about two hours' walk from the trailhead. A superb view awaited us there. There was almost no wind, and on the eerily still surface of the lake were reflected steep mountains carved by glaciers over long ages. The marine-blue, or perhaps emerald-green, lake was so still that it seemed less a lake than a huge mirror laid on the ground. By the way, from the trailhead to here, we hadn't passed a single hiker. Who we did meet were the little residents of the Canadian Rockies, squirrels. The guidebook said Canadian squirrels aren't very afraid of people, and it was true: they kept popping their heads out from both sides of the trail and delighting us.

This is a rest shelter in a corner of the campground beside the lake. Here a few hikers came down from above. I'm not a fan of hikes crowded with people, but having no people at all is frightening in its own way. We were relieved to finally pass someone.
From Kinney Lake we walked on further north. In the centre of the far-left photo above is a cute chipmunk.
This stretch was a bit tough for us, having been short on exercise lately. Our destination was Berg Lake, but we decided to camp at a campground past three waterfalls.

Tonight's dinner was a Japanese-style rice bowl with a thick savoury sauce. Mao had worked out the recipe back in Japan. Some of the ingredients we brought from Japan and some we bought locally. Vegetable prices seemed about the same as in Japan, but meat was frighteningly cheap. Perfect for storing up fat.
The cold at night was very severe, and Mao seemed to have caught a cold. Going further tomorrow would be too hard, so we decided to turn back.
Day 5 (8 Sep) — Coming down
Mt. Robson Provincial Park to Jasper

We got up while it was still dark and set off for the trailhead in the morning mist. Yesterday clouds came in from the afternoon and we couldn't see Robson, but today it was fairly clear and we could see Robson's west face. Truly a sheer cliff.

The trailhead was close. With Robson and its permanent snow at our backs, we headed for the trailhead. The squirrels came out for us again today. Apparently many kinds of squirrel live in the Canadian Rockies, including chipmunks and ground squirrels.
We came down safely. A commemorative photo in front of the visitor centre with Mt. Robson behind us.

Today's destination was Jasper in Alberta. As it's in a national park, you have to pay an entry fee at a gate near the provincial border. In Jasper too we decided to stay at a campground: Whistlers Campground, at the foot of Whistlers Mountain, a short drive south of the town. This one also has huge grounds, like a big nature theme park. The photo on the upper left is our living space. There's probably enough land to build a house. We couldn't hike until Mao's cold got better, so we decided to stay two nights here.
Day 6 (9 Sep) — Taking it easy at the campground
Whistlers Campground

Today we took it easy at the campground in Jasper. Whistlers Campground is also of a very high standard, fully equipped with hot showers. Staying in the tent all day was boring, so we headed into the town of Jasper. There are several tourist towns in the Canadian Rockies, but the famous ones are Banff and Jasper. Banff apparently gets lots of Japanese tourists, but Jasper doesn't have so many visitors and is a very calm town; I liked it a lot. For lunch we ordered a Papa Burger and Mozza Burger combo at the burger chain A&W. In Canada there seem to be more A&Ws than McDonald's. You don't see McDonald's much in country towns, whereas I felt there's an A&W in practically any town of 1,000 people.
Then we went to the visitor centre to get information about hiking from tomorrow, and there we learned a shocking fact.

On this trip, besides the Berg Lake Trail, we planned to do one more: the Skyline Trail, the most famous in Jasper National Park, said to have superb views because it's so high. But perhaps because of that very height, it was already closed by snow this year. We had neither the gear nor the knowledge for snowy mountains. We had no choice but to give up, and decided to skip hiking tomorrow and head for Edmonton.

After sightseeing in town, we came back to the campground. Our site had a table like the one in the photo above, so today we cooked outside. Cooking in the thick coniferous forest felt open and was great fun ♪ The frying pan we bought at MEC was not only light but non-stick! While we were happily cooking...

Mao's face suddenly froze and she cried, "What's that!" Looking, a huge brown creature was walking leisurely ahead of us. It seemed to be a wild elk. At first I thought it was a pet kept on the grounds, but that couldn't be. Looking closely, there were several more elk. The other guests looked at them and chatted, "It's a family", without seeming surprised at all.
Day 7 (10 Sep) — Edmonton, city of oil
Jasper to Edmonton

We gave up on hiking the Skyline Trail, but at its trailhead is Maligne Lake, known for its scenery, so we decided to at least see that before heading to Edmonton, even though it was in the other direction. The weather was pleasantly sunny, and from viewpoints along the way we could see the majestic Canadian Rockies continuing forever. In Canada the speed limit outside cities is around 100 km/h, the roads are wide with nothing in the way, and it's really pleasant to drive.

Some cloud came in so the photo is dark, but this is Maligne Lake, said to be the most typical glacial lake around here. As you can see, there's already a lot of snow on the mountains behind. Winter comes early.
Is it too small to make out? Here too we found a cute squirrel.
This is the Skyline Trail trailhead. We didn't finish the Berg Lake Trail either; I want to come back someday!!

Leaving Maligne Lake, we headed for Edmonton. The mountainous Rockies had many peaks with jagged, saw-like ridges, but east of the range is the great plains. Edmonton is right in the middle of the plain, so it gets flatter and flatter as you approach. On the way we had lunch in a town called Edson.

We plunged into Edmonton. A city landscape for the first time in a while. We tried to go to a cheap motel we had found in advance, the Chateau Motel, but although we knew where it was, we took a wrong turn by a hair. We were on a freeway, so we had to keep driving toward Calgary for a while, and came back along a muddy Local Only road, which got the car dirty. Tonight's motel was an exceptional price, about 6,000 yen a night for two. For that, it even had a kitchen; comfortable!
The kitchen and the outside of the motel. Canadian motels almost all have free wireless internet, which is handy. I had brought a netbook, so we could look up maps of the next day's roads online.
Day 8 (11 Sep) — West Edmonton Mall, a paradise in a frozen land

Today we went to one of the highlights of the trip, West Edmonton Mall. It's a shopping mall like a giant version of Aeon in Japan. Apparently it's one of the largest in North America, a facility that realised the ideal of Edmonton residents who live with harsh winters. It has over 900 shops, plus an indoor water park and even an amusement park.

The amusement park seemed very much for small children, so this time we just walked through. There's no admission charge. The classic scenario is probably the husband bringing the kids here while the wife enjoys shopping.
Canadian McDonald's has a maple leaf in the middle of the M.

Cars were on display all over the mall. The Lamborghini on the far right is a luxury sports car worth tens of millions of yen, but it's not for sale; it will be given to the winner of a draw among customers who entered.
That day a live concert was being held where the skating rink normally is. It was very popular.
There was an indoor pool, a sea lion show stage, and even a mini aquarium.
Today's lunch was KFC.
Japanese sushi seems to be a major food here too. And we had dessert at Yogen Früz, which has recently come to Japan too. It's far cheaper here, and you get more! Why is Japan so stingy...
It was show time, so we went to watch the sea lion show. Watching close up costs money, but watching from a little distance is free.
Trampolines right next to the indoor pool. It does look fun, but wouldn't it be quite embarrassing to just keep bouncing for 10 minutes in front of a crowd?

Tonight's dinner was a real luxury: teppanyaki! I think it was about 3,000 yen each. The steak, using AAA-grade Alberta beef sirloin, tasted exceptional. This restaurant is actually Japanese Village, which we also visited a year and a half ago. The chef cooked for us while emphasising Japan at every turn, but with the familiar knife-twirling performance and the DJ-like live patter, it seemed to have gone beyond Japan altogether. It's not just the meat: their pride is the sauce, rich with sesame. Great poured over rice too! A place I'll always want to visit when I come to Edmonton. Sadly, the Japanese woman who was there on a working holiday last year was gone.
Day 9 (12 Sep) — The indoor pool
to Valleyview

Today we said goodbye to Edmonton and began heading north toward the far north at last, but first we went back to the mall we visited yesterday to swim in the indoor pool. The rink where the concert was held yesterday had been completely cleared of equipment, and customers were elegantly skating on the ice.

This is the indoor pool. Not too many people, not too few; the slides only had queues of a few minutes. We relaxed in the wave pool, jacuzzi and so on. At the back of the left photo is a bungee jump said to have the highest drop of any indoors in the world. Just before someone jumps, a siren sounds through the whole building, and they dive with everyone's eyes on them. If you chicken out and don't jump, boos are guaranteed.
Leaving the city where we had recovered from tent life, we headed for Valleyview and tonight's lodging, the High Valley Motor Inn. The clouds didn't look good, and it rained several times.

There was a restaurant near the motel, but to save money we went to a supermarket in town and bought ready-made food. The 6-piece cheese that's essential with beer in Japan was sold as 12-piece cheese in Canada.
Good night...
Day 10 (13 Sep) — Autumn arrives
Valleyview to Fort Nelson
We left the motel and headed north-west. Today we crossed the border from Alberta back into British Columbia.

Past Grande Prairie, a fair-sized town, and further west. The broadleaf forests on both sides of the endless highway were already turning yellow, announcing autumn. Out here there was hardly any traffic, and houses and other man-made things were sparse. There was roadwork along the way. In Canada, with its long winters, roadwork is apparently concentrated in the summer.
Oh, we crossed the border...
Yellow fields of flowers spreading across the vast plain, a flock of sheep. For me, everything felt good.
We weren't in the far north yet, but here we saw a Yukon licence plate for the first time!

Northern British Columbia. Gentle green hills go on forever. What I had felt ever since coming inland was how extreme the temperature swings are. Mornings are cold enough to make you shiver, so the autumn colours make sense, but by midday it's warm and sunny. Drive with the windows shut and it's hot enough to sweat. And the days are still long; the sun seems to stay at almost the same height from morning to evening. Even at noon it doesn't climb high, and even after it sets at night it takes a long time to get dark. This happens because the sun sets at a slant to the horizon.
We were driving smoothly toward Fort Nelson, but about 100 km before it the road suddenly became unpaved. The speed limit dropped to 50 km/h, and the slow traffic continued until the paving returned.

Whether it was under construction or the asphalt hadn't been laid yet, the unpaved stretch of several dozen kilometres ended ☆ The smoothness of tarmac was a blessing. Foot down again and a quick 100 km/h.

We arrived at our lodging: a cheap-looking motel we found by searching around town. Tonight's motel was also clean and comfortable. For dinner we bought ready-made food at a supermarket in the Save-On-Foods group. Fruit juice and cut salad are handy for getting vitamins easily. Fast food and meat every day just stores up fat. We had packed away the tent we lived in in the Canadian Rockies while it was still damp, so to stop it going mouldy we hung it over the car overnight to dry.
Day 11 (14 Sep) — Arctic Canada (the far north)
Fort Nelson to Watson Lake
Pleasantly sunny from the morning. But very cold... The tent we hung out to dry had instead got wet with morning dew. In the sun it soon dried crisp again.

Breakfast today was burgers at A&W again. We'd been given coupons at the branch in the Edmonton shopping mall, so we could eat very cheaply. Three dollars each is plenty to fill you up. A&W seems more particular about meat than McDonald's; there's nothing like a Filet-O-Fish, and every burger has meat. We never ended up eating it on this trip, but the triple-patty Grandpa Burger is something else.

The scenery was so good we kept stopping the car. As we kept heading north, the average temperature seemed to be dropping steadily. You could clearly see the autumn colours advancing. Unlike in Japan, you hardly see any red in Canadian autumn leaves. It's almost all yellow, and looked as if golden carpets had been laid here and there.

The view from Summit Pass. Far in the distance we could see a pure-white mountain range. Still only September, and they were completely snowy mountains. Probably part of the Northern Canadian Rockies. We were about to plunge into a wilderness covered in permanent snow.
As we drove, something moved at the roadside. Stopping the car, we saw a deer-like creature eating grass. It stared at us, but made no attempt to run.
The contrast between the autumn leaves and the snowy mountains was beautiful. Depending on altitude, the white parts covered in snow and the black parts of bare mountainside were clearly divided.
We met animals again! This time a herd. A family of mule deer with young, perhaps.

This time a family of goats. Even when we stopped the car, they paid us no attention at all. Nothing in particular seemed to be lying on the road, but they showed no interest in anything else and just kept eating something.
Another animal encounter. A short-antlered moose, or perhaps... Once we entered the mountains, we suddenly started meeting animals. The Canadian Rockies really are a paradise for large wildlife.
Perhaps because of the high latitude, the mountains gradually lost their trees entirely. Bare black mountainsides were exposed.

Some cloud came in. A short break on the shore of Muncho Lake. Looking at the information board, bison appear around here. The article said several are killed every year in traffic accidents. From the photo, they're big with scary faces. Last year too we often saw "Watch for bison" road signs in the far north, but never actually saw a bison. Probably there are few of them and you rarely meet one...

Or so I thought, for a moment. A little way on from the rest stop, black dots appeared ahead, and as we got closer they turned out to be a herd of bison!! We were overwhelmed by their huge numbers. But they were occupying the road, which was quite a nuisance. I honked to get them to move, but of course human common sense doesn't work on them, and they didn't budge at all. Seconds after honking, their total lack of reaction filled me with fear that this was a bad idea. If they charged us, there was no doubt we would suffer serious damage, even inside the car.
Just before Watson Lake we finally crossed 60° north. North of here is called the far north, a land of extreme cold.

We arrived at Watson Lake. Few buildings, and we couldn't tell where the supermarket was; we had come somewhere very remote. After driving hundreds of kilometres from Fort Nelson, to find only a place this remote. Tonight's lodging, the Air Force Lodge, was a very clean log building. The rooms were small, and the bath and toilet were shared, but it was cleaned thoroughly and the owner was friendly. After settling in a bit, we went into town to eat dinner, but couldn't find anything like a restaurant, so we ate a hot meal at the motel's restaurant.
Day 12 (15 Sep) — A hot spring in the far north
Watson Lake to Whitehorse (Takhini Hot Springs)
We set off for Whitehorse, the capital of the Yukon. Good weather again today, following yesterday.

As far as the eye could see, magnificent scenery seemingly untouched by people. Beyond the coniferous forest was a shapely mountain. And a river flowing slowly through the forest. The autumn colours grew even more vivid, and the trees glowing orange were so beautiful we couldn't stop staring.
Before the town of Teslin we crossed a big river. A scenic place surrounded by autumn leaves.

Driving further on from Teslin, I wanted to take a photo of the endless straight road, so I stopped at the roadside and set up the camera on a tripod. Just then I suddenly needed to pee, so I left Mao asleep in the car and went a little way into the conifers beside the road. When I came back a few minutes later, Mao was outside the car crying. She said that when she woke up nobody was there, with only the tripod left outside, she thought I had been eaten by an elk or a bear and cried from fear. From now on I'll have to be careful not to do confusing things.
We arrived in Whitehorse. Relief at a city with buildings for the first time in a while.

We stocked up at a big supermarket in town. We'd be camping more from now on, including tonight, and thought there wouldn't be many shops, so we bought in bulk. We wanted to make curry rice, but searched everywhere and couldn't find roux. After a while we found Japanese curry roux. The thought of enjoying a Japanese taste for the first time in ages was exciting. Around this Glico curry roux were other Japanese products too, like wasabi and Pocky. They had sushi vinegar, but no ordinary vinegar.

Takhini Hot Springs is in the outskirts, about 30 minutes' drive from downtown Whitehorse. Our scheme was to watch the aurora while soaking in the hot spring. There is a campground on the hot-spring grounds, and tonight we pitched our tent and stayed here. Today's campground was spacious too, a peaceful place surrounded by trees like birch. Many people in Canada travel by camper van, and at the campgrounds so far, including this one, there were sites with power outlets for them. You can't leave your engine running all night, so camper-van people run a cable from their vehicle and take power from the outlet to run the heating or cook. It's like taking your whole house with you. You do see it in Japan too, but in Canada there really were lots of camper-van travellers.

Tonight I tried to make something like a cream stew with what we had bought at lunchtime, but I messed up the cooking and burnt it, and it tasted terrible. It was my own fault for turning all the burners to maximum.

After dinner we pulled ourselves together and got in the hot spring. You wear a swimsuit, so it's mixed, with a cooler area you could stay in for hours and a hot area like a Japanese hot spring. Stay in the hot area too long and you get dizzy, so we went back and forth between the two, enjoying a hot spring in the far north and waiting for the aurora. But having come to such a high latitude, the days are that much longer. It stayed light until after 9 p.m., and in the end we couldn't see the aurora. Even if it had been out, I think the surrounding lights would have got in the way a bit.
Back at the tent we looked up at the night sky several times, but the aurora didn't come out for us.
Day 13 (16 Sep) — The Gold Rush town
to Dawson City

From Takhini Hot Springs we drove almost due north along the Klondike Highway, following the Yukon River. About a hundred years ago gold was found in the Klondike, starting what is known as the Gold Rush.

Around Fox Lake a forest fire apparently broke out more than ten years ago, and an information board at the rest stop explained the damage at the time. In fact, burnt trees were still standing without having fallen. After this too we saw many signs saying "Forest fire, year XX". The air is dry, so fires may start easily.
There is nothing you could call a town between Whitehorse and Dawson. Just small settlements and petrol stations. Otherwise you just keep driving through forest.
At the rest stops on the Klondike Highway there were information boards with trivia from the Gold Rush days. From a rest stop on slightly higher ground we could see the horizon of the forest.

We played a little at a river before Dawson while taking a break. It was only for a short time, so I stayed in short sleeves, but it was by no means warm. The water was cold, and I couldn't bring myself to get in and play. On top of that, if we met a grizzly that had come for the salmon, we'd have to be prepared to die.

We decided to stay at a motel on the outskirts of Dawson City. We expected it to be expensive since it's so remote, but surprisingly it wasn't: under 100 dollars for two. Motels never let us down! A strong ally on the trip.

After a rest at the motel, we explored the town. Now the amount of gold being found has dropped completely, and the town has declined into a ghost town. Abandoned buildings that nobody seems to live in are scattered about, and apparently these ruins are now a tourist attraction. It was a town that made me very sad.

We ate at a restaurant in town, and on the way back to the motel we found an intriguing road called Dome Road and decided to try it. At the end of a long climb, a spectacular viewpoint awaited, looking out over Dawson and everything around. Let's come back here when it's dark and wait for the aurora.
There was still plenty of time until dark, so we did laundry in the room.

After 10 p.m., it finally got dark, so we went out to that spot. The aurora, faintly visible even before we reached the top, broke up after we waited a while!! It performed an elegant dance in a night sky full of stars.
Day 14 (17 Sep) — The Dempster Highway and the tundra
to Tombstone Territorial Park

About 20 minutes' drive back from Dawson City toward Whitehorse is the junction with the Dempster Highway, which runs further north. The Dempster Highway, over 700 km long, is Canada's northernmost road. It ends at the town of Inuvik on the Arctic Ocean, close to 70° north, inside the Arctic Circle. The original final destination of the trip was Inuvik, but since we had changed plans several times and the distance was getting hard, we decided not to go to the end, but to drive as far as Tombstone Territorial Park along the way and come back. Today's destination was Tombstone Territorial Park, just over 100 km from the start of the Dempster Highway. A little past the junction, a bridge with a wooden deck marks the start of the Dempster Highway.

A few minutes from the start, the paving ends and the unpaved section begins. Apparently it stays unpaved all the way to the end. And before Inuvik you cross the Peel River and the Mackenzie River on free ferries in summer. In winter the rivers freeze completely, so you can drive on ice roads over them. On our last visit, we crossed the Mackenzie River ice road before Yellowknife. Along the way we saw several ptarmigans. We were driving at nearly 100 km/h, so if you spot one you have to slow down immediately or you might run it over. The ptarmigans have almost no wariness and don't run even when you approach. They had camouflage colouring that blends into the plants, like the ones you sometimes see in the Japanese Alps in summer. On our last visit in winter, these too were a beautiful pure white.

Continuing north for a while, we came into tundra where plants are sparse. From late August to early September, for a very short period, the ground here turns golden and red. It's called tundra foliage, and you can only see it in tundra regions. We had been hoping for this, but sadly it seemed we were a few days late this time. The peak had passed; we could see yellow and red here and there, but overall it looked brownish.
It's very dry, so the very occasional truck we passed kicked up huge clouds of dust.

Tombstone Territorial Park. Trees can't grow there; it is truly one of the frontiers of the Earth, where only a very few living things are allowed to live: lichens such as mosses, and animals like caribou, musk oxen and lemmings that have adapted to the extreme cold. A few hundred kilometres north of here is the Arctic Circle, the region of the midnight sun in summer, when the sun doesn't set, and the polar night in winter, when the sun doesn't rise.

Faced with a view like this, you want to get even a little closer. We shouldered our packs and decided to aim for the top of the mountain at the back. I don't know its name. If there's a mountain, a wandervogel club member's instinct is to want to climb it. The ground was muddy, with streams flowing here and there. This is said to be the biggest bear habitat in Canada, so we had to be careful. We walked for a while, but the mountain never got any closer, and because of the time we gave up on the summit. How pathetic...
We decided to camp at an unmanned campground in the park. It was very cold, so to keep warm we gathered fallen wood and leaves to make a fire, and started cooking.
Today's menu was curry rice using ingredients bought at the supermarket in Whitehorse. Curry rice with that nostalgic Japanese taste was superb!

Even though it was unmanned, the toilets were maintained, and there was even a box for paying. We paid properly and registered. It's really something to be grateful for that they maintain a campground in a land that's cold even in summer. There was only one other group besides us. The sun was slow to set; only after 10 p.m. did night finally come to this land.
Day 15 (18 Sep) — Heading back
Tombstone Territorial Park to Whitehorse (Takhini Hot Springs)
From today we turned for home, aiming for Vancouver far to the south. Probably about 3,000 km away.

A short break on the Klondike Highway. Walking to the river flowing right beside us, we found footprints of some animal on the slightly muddy riverbank. It might have been a dog, but the footprints were quite large, so perhaps a bear. In fact, later while driving we saw a bear. It just dashed across the road ahead, so we couldn't get a photo.
A little further south, we could see places where faint autumn colours still remained. Back along the Yukon River toward Whitehorse.

Just over 600 km from our starting point, after driving through the wilderness, we were back in the capital, Whitehorse. Around here we saw lots of cars with Alaska plates too. We went to the same supermarket as before and bought pork steaks. Actually, last time we bought the same meat and made ginger pork at Takhini Hot Springs. We couldn't forget the taste, so we decided to make it again.

Besides Alaska plates, we also spotted a Northwest Territories plate shaped like a polar bear. Inuvik, at the end of the Dempster Highway, is not in the Yukon but in the Northwest Territories. Or perhaps they came from the Great Slave Lake side.

After that, at Walmart, the famous North American store that sells everything, I bought sandals. The shoes I brought from Japan had been worn so constantly that they gave off a strange smell. Then we stopped at the visitor centre and went back to Takhini Hot Springs. I burned the smelly shoes as fuel for the campfire.
Pork sizzling on the grill. Ginger pork made with pork steaks is superb. By the way, in Canada beef and pork cost about the same; in fact beef was even a bit cheaper.

After dinner, the hot spring again today. Amazing that it's 8 at night and still this light! With it this bright, there's no way you'd see the aurora. Unlike Japanese hot springs, it's mixed and you wear swimsuits. As big as a pool. There were lots of couples, and one couple kept up passionate kisses the whole time without caring at all about the people around them.
Day 16 (19 Sep) — Northern British Columbia
to Dease Lake
Breakfast at A&W again this morning.

The autumn colours were still beautiful. But getting bored of this scenery, or doing nothing but gaze at it, could bring a repeat of last year's tragic accident. It's on the way back that you let your guard down. Let's be really careful on the way home.

Just before Watson Lake we left the Alaska Highway and joined Highway 37, heading south toward British Columbia. Soon we crossed the border into the far north of British Columbia. Vancouver is in the same province, but it's bigger than Japan, so the distance is mind-boggling.
Highway 37: since it's called a highway, we expected a fast two-lane road with a 100 km/h limit, but it had no centre line, steep ups and downs and lots of curves.

We kept driving along a lonely road that almost no cars use. There were places like settlements, but no facilities to stay in, and we got anxious. In a small settlement of a few hundred people called Dease Lake we found a motel and went in. We thought it would be very expensive, but it was about 100 dollars, a relief. A clean, comfortable room with lots of natural light through big windows. Dinner was at the nearby restaurant, the only restaurant in this settlement. Here we ordered rainbow trout and salmon set meals.
Day 17 (20 Sep) — South
Dease Lake to Smithers

Dease Lake was without doubt the smallest town so far. And it was unimaginably cold. The proof: when we went back to the car in the morning, the cut salad we had bought a few days before was frozen...
Like yesterday, we drove a road with a beautiful contrast between autumn leaves and snowy mountains.

There was nothing like a town at all, but for some reason an airfield stood all alone. One helicopter was parked there, but there was nobody around. No control tower either; it seemed to be a completely unmanned airfield.

There were no petrol stations on Highway 37 until the small town just before it joins Highway 16. That was a big miscalculation, and the fuel gauge got low enough for the warning light to come on. Running out of fuel on a road with so little traffic would be serious. From now on I must make sure to refuel with plenty of margin!
Major roadworks underway.

After joining Highway 16 we drove about 100 km east and arrived in the town of Smithers. For the first time in quite a while we had come to a town where, if not a city, I could imagine living. There are plenty of places to eat, A&W included. At the supermarket we bought a risotto-like dish you just heat in the microwave, and frankfurters, and decided to eat at the motel. Tonight's lodging, the Florence Motel, had a kitchen. All the kitchens in Canadian lodgings had electric hobs rather than gas like in Japan. Electric, but not the induction hobs of Japan: the type where a coiled heating element glows red-hot.
Day 18 (21 Sep) — Trans-Canada Highway 16
Smithers to Prince George
A lovely morning. Breakfast today at our favourite A&W. We still had coupons left from Edmonton.

Today's leg was short. We drove about 300 km along roads where the autumn leaves were still beautiful and arrived in Prince George, a city of about 100,000. Prince George really is a transport hub: south to Vancouver, west to Prince Rupert on the Pacific, east to the Rocky Mountains, and north to the far north. The main roads in all four directions meet in this city.

For the next two nights we stayed at the Prince Motel, which we had looked up in Japan. It was one of the cheapest motels we used; booking online in advance made it just 49 dollars a night. But being cheap didn't mean it was shabby: it was as clean and comfortable as the motels so far.
Our clothes were getting dirty, so we went to a coin laundry we found online. In America and Canada a coin laundry is called a Laundromat. Apparently it's a word made from laundry and automatic.
Mao cleaning the windscreen with all her might.
Perhaps out of concern for the environment, the cheapest regular petrol had a sticker saying ethanol was added.
Day 19 (22 Sep) — A rest day

We had been driving every day until now, but today we decided to take it easy, exploring Prince George for the day. The shopping centre about a ten-minute walk from the motel wasn't very big, but it had familiar shops like Save-On-Foods. This shopping centre also had a dollar store, where we bought Canada goods and other souvenirs for ourselves.
Day 20 (23 Sep) — To the metropolis
to Vancouver
Our road trip, covering about 7,000 km, was finally reaching its climax. The day had come to return to Vancouver, Canada's third-largest city.
Thinking this would be the last we'd see of this peaceful Canadian countryside, a reluctance to leave welled up.

What I thought while driving in Canada is that there are so many lakes. Not only huge lakes like Great Slave Lake near Yellowknife and Great Bear Lake further north, but especially in the north it's a lake district dotted with lakes of all sizes. Heading steadily south from Prince George, near Cache Creek, the junction town for Kamloops, bare hills with sparse trees began to dominate the scenery. It didn't seem like an area with so little rain; why had it become all bare hills like this?
South of Cache Creek, Trans-Canada Highway 1 was the opposite of what we expected: a road through the mountains. There were also many tunnels, which you hardly ever see in Canada.

Closer and closer to Vancouver. In the town of Hope we passed the petrol station where, on last year's trip, the Jeep suddenly made strange noises and sprayed liquid. Fortunately on this trip we'd had no accidents, not even a scrape, and no breakdowns. I hope we can get back to Seattle safely like this, and at the end give the car a good wash at a car wash as a thank-you.

Driving on toward Vancouver, we joined Highway 5 coming from Kamloops. The road immediately got better and the land turned to plains. Towns like Abbotsford already felt like the city. Eventually the skyscrapers of downtown Vancouver came into view.

We went to the Palms Motel on Kingsway, a little away from downtown Vancouver. This motel had a completely different atmosphere from the lodgings so far. The interior had a somewhat Chinese feel, and the receptionist was Asian too. And around the motel, shops with signs in Chinese and Korean lined the streets. Streets that made you wonder whether you were really in Canada.

Until we reached Vancouver, we had checked our wallets many times, been careful not to run into money trouble, and kept economising, because we expected lodging in Vancouver to be very expensive. But the Palms Motel cost far less than expected, under 100 dollars a night. We were going to have quite a lot of money left over, and suddenly we felt generous. We had cut back on food in particular, so today we treated ourselves to a Korean barbecue restaurant. The customers were all Asian, and though I've never been, the barbecue was probably just like in Korea. The kimchi was good too, and for some reason Japanese sashimi was on the menu, so we ordered it. It was the best dinner.
Day 21 (24 Sep) — Shopping (1)
The next day it was raining from the morning. Happily we had more money left over than we could spend, so breakfast was a luxurious Starbucks!
First, straight to Granville Island to enjoy some shopping. You can see the downtown skyline of towering high-rises too.
Bought earrings, a knit hat and a hoodie ♪

Tonight was nostalgic Japanese food: sushi! A place called Tsunami Sushi on Robson Street downtown doesn't stand out much, but perhaps it's well known, as it was busy with lots of people. Unlike Japanese conveyor-belt sushi, the sushi floats past on little boats. Sushi made with fresh tuna, squid, scallop and so on was as good as anything in Japan. The raw oysters especially were superb, dressed with a vinegar that suited them well. But it wasn't as reasonable as 100-yen sushi in Japan; the bill came to about 6,000 yen for two... We had no intention of changing our Canadian dollars back into yen, so fine, but back in Japan we probably won't be this extravagant for a long while.
The extravagance didn't stop (lol). Dessert to finish at a gelato shop listed in our guidebook.

From downtown Vancouver you can clearly see Cypress Mountain, a venue of the 2010 Vancouver Olympics. At night the lights halfway up the mountain stand out. We thought if we went up there we'd see a really beautiful night view, so we drove. Crossing the Lions Gate Bridge and climbing the mountain, there was a viewpoint with a few cars parked, and from there we could enjoy an astonishingly beautiful night view of Vancouver. There were a few other couples, and now and then we heard Japanese. Glancing over, it seemed to be a couple of a Canadian man and a Japanese woman. Surely he was a boyfriend she met while studying abroad, who had brought her in his car. She was being wooed in sweet English...
Day 22 (25 Sep) — Returning the rental car
Vancouver ⇔ Seattle

For about three weeks, the Elantra had carried us really well. Over 8,000 km. Having kept going without a single problem, the Elantra's body was covered in mud. As a thank-you, at the end we gave it the top car wash at a petrol station. In Canada, with its harsh winters, brush-type washes like in Japan would freeze and scratch the body, so this one sprayed colourful cleaning agents as in the photo and then washed with powerful water pressure alone. Sparkling clean, the Elantra looked somehow proud. Hyundai of Korea has grown astonishingly in the last few years. This Elantra, combining performance and low price, is said to be selling explosively, on course to overtake the Toyota Corolla and Honda Civic.
Heading for the US border.

Just before the border inspection there's a duty-free shop, much like at an airport. We bought the familiar maple cookies and T-shirts. To stop people driving the wrong way, in front of the duty-free car park there were spikes that would puncture your tyres if you reversed.
A long queue in front of the inspection booths.
We arrived at our old friend, the Seattle branch of Budget rent-a-car. The return procedure was very simple. Goodbye, Elantra.
Seattle was blessed with clear skies, and it seemed warmer than on our last visit. Parted from our partner, we headed to the bus depot feeling an indescribable emptiness.
While waiting for the bus at the depot, we bought gum with leftover money. It tasted so intense we never finished it.

After getting back to Vancouver, we went to a Chinese restaurant near the motel for dinner. Perhaps because it was originally a Chinatown, almost all the other customers were Chinese, and lively Chinese echoed through the restaurant. The portions were enormous for the price!
Day 23 (26 Sep) — Shopping (2)

Tomorrow we had to leave Canada and fly home to Japan. Today was our last day to enjoy shopping in Vancouver. From downtown we took the boat called the SeaBus to Lonsdale Quay Public Market in North Vancouver.

The first place we stopped at in the market was a seafood shop called Mimi's. They not only sell lobster, crab and oysters direct, but if you ask they'll steam them for you right there in a steamer. We had them steam big oysters and fresh crab that was moving in the tank. Needless to say, the super-fresh oysters and crab were delicious.
We ordered clam chowder too.
We bought dessert at a fruit shop where you can fill a cup with as much fresh fruit as you like. For dinner we went to Tsunami Sushi on Robson Street again.
Days 24–25 (27–28 Sep) — Going home
to Japan via U.S.A.

The day to go home had come at last. Honestly, I didn't want to go back. If I could speak English better, it's a country I seriously thought I'd like to live in one day. From the motel we had to go to the airport carrying a mountain of luggage.

We had been to A&W many times, but never once to Tim Hortons, so we decided to spend our last Canadian dollars at the branch in the airport. We thought it would be enough, but because of tax it came to slightly more. We paid the shortfall by credit card. The amount: 20 cents. I felt bad about that.
To Seattle it was the same small Horizon Air propeller plane as on the way out.
Farewell! Canada...
After taking off from Seattle, we could look down on the city from above. The tower that symbolises the city looked tiny too.
We passed over Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. We could see countless small islands. From the air they looked uninhabited.
We arrived safely in Japan. What awaited us back home was our graduation research and job hunting.
